title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: In the Surovsky district there was no railway and no post-horse service, so Levin drove there with his own horses in his big, old-fashioned carriage.

He stopped halfway at a well-off peasant's to feed his horses. A bald, well-preserved old man with a broad red beard going gray on his cheeks opened the gate, squeezing against the gatepost to let the three horses pass. He directed the coachman to a place under the shed in the big, clean, tidy yard with its charred, old-fashioned plows, and asked Levin to come into the parlor. A neatly dressed young woman, with clogs on her bare feet, was scrubbing the floor of the new outer room. She was startled by the dog, who ran in after Levin, and gave a shriek, but burst out laughing at her own fright as soon as she was told the dog wouldn't hurt her. Pointing the way to the parlor door with her bare arm, she bent down again, hiding her handsome face, and went on scrubbing.
"Would you like the samovar?" she asked.
"Yes, please."

The parlor was a big room with a Dutch stove and a screen dividing it in two. Under the holy pictures stood a table painted in patterns, a bench, and two chairs. Near the entrance was a dresser full of crockery. The shutters were closed, there were few flies, and the room was so clean that Levin worried Laska — who had been running along the road and bathing in puddles — would dirty the floor, and ordered her to a corner near the door. After looking around the parlor, Levin went out into the back yard. The good-looking young woman in clogs, swinging the empty pails on her yoke, ran ahead of him to the well for water.

"Look sharp, my girl!" the old man called after her good-humoredly, and he came over to Levin. "So, sir, are you on your way to Nikolay Ivanovitch Sviazhsky? His honor stops by here too," he began, leaning his elbows on the steps' railing and settling in for a chat. In the middle of the old man's account of his acquaintance with Sviazhsky, the gates creaked again, and laborers came into the yard from the fields with wooden plows and harrows. The horses harnessed to them were sleek and fat. The laborers were plainly of the household: two were young men in cotton shirts and caps, and the other two were hired laborers in homespun shirts — one an old man, the other a young fellow. Moving off from the steps, the old man went over to the horses and began unharnessing them.
"What have they been plowing?" Levin asked.
"Plowing up the potatoes. We rent a bit of land too. Fedot, don't let out the gelding — take him to the trough; we'll put the other one in harness."
"Father, the plowshares I ordered — has he brought them?" asked the big, healthy-looking fellow, plainly the old man's son.
"There — in the outer room," the old man answered, gathering up the harness he had taken off and flinging it on the ground. "You can fit them on while they have dinner."

The good-looking young woman came into the outer room with the full pails tugging at her shoulders. More women appeared from somewhere — young and handsome, middle-aged, old and ugly, with children and without.
The samovar began to sing; the laborers and the family, finished with the horses, came in for dinner. Levin got his provisions out of his carriage and invited the old man to take tea with him.
"Well, I've had some today already," said the old man, plainly accepting with pleasure. "But just a glass for company."

Over tea Levin heard all about the old man's farming. Ten years before, the old man had rented three hundred acres from the lady who owned them, and a year ago he had bought them outright and rented another three hundred from a neighboring landowner. A small part — the worst part — he let out for rent, while a hundred acres of arable land he cultivated himself with his family and two hired laborers. The old man complained that things were going badly. But Levin could see he was complaining out of a sense of decorum, and that his farm was in flourishing shape. If it hadn't been, he wouldn't have bought land at thirty-five roubles the acre, wouldn't have married off three sons and a nephew, wouldn't have rebuilt twice after fires — and each time on a larger scale. In spite of the complaints, it was plain that he was proud, and justly proud, of his prosperity, proud of his sons, his nephew, his sons' wives, his horses and cows, and most of all proud of holding the whole operation together. From his conversation with the old man, Levin thought he was not averse to new methods either. He had planted a great many potatoes, and his potatoes — as Levin had seen driving past — were already past flowering and starting to die down, while Levin's were only just coming into flower. He earthed up his potatoes with a modern plow borrowed from a neighboring landowner. He sowed wheat. The small fact that, when thinning his rye, the old man used the rye he thinned out as horse feed especially struck Levin. How many times Levin had seen this splendid fodder wasted and tried to get it saved; but it had always turned out to be impossible. The peasant got it done and couldn't praise it enough as feed for the beasts.
"What have the wenches to do? They carry it out in bundles to the roadside, and the cart brings it away."
"Well, we landowners can't manage well with our laborers," said Levin, passing him a glass of tea.

"Thank you," said the old man, taking the glass but refusing sugar, pointing at a lump he still had. "They're sheer ruin," he said. "Look at Sviazhsky's, for instance. We know what the land's like — first-rate — and yet there's not much of a crop to brag about. It isn't looked after — that's all it comes to!"
"But you work your land with hired laborers?"
"We're all peasants together. We go into everything ourselves. If a man's no use, he can go, and we'll manage on our own."
"Father, Finogen wants some tar," said the young woman in the clogs, coming in.
"Yes, yes, that's how it is, sir!" the old man said, getting up; and crossing himself deliberately, he thanked Levin and went out.

When Levin went into the kitchen to call his coachman, he saw the whole family at dinner. The women were standing up waiting on them. The young, sturdy-looking son was telling some funny story with his mouth full of pudding, and they were all laughing — the woman in the clogs, ladling cabbage soup into a bowl, laughing the most merrily of all.

Very likely the good-looking face of the young woman in clogs had a great deal to do with the sense of well-being this peasant household gave Levin, but the impression was so strong that Levin couldn't shake it off. All the way from the old peasant's to Sviazhsky's he kept turning back to this peasant farm, as though there were something in the impression that demanded special attention from him.
